Orthonormal sum-to-zero contrasts

Source: R/facets.R
contr_sum_zero.Rd

Contrasts for a factor whose effects should sum to zero, with the same prior variance for every level. Useful for small facets, such as a few items or raters, modelled as fixed effects in a many-facet Rasch model.

Usage

contr_sum_zero(n, contrasts = TRUE, sparse = FALSE)

Arguments

n

The number of levels, or a vector of level labels (for example levels(x)), as in stats::contr.sum().

contrasts

If FALSE, one indicator column per level is returned instead, as for stats::contr.sum(). R uses this for factors without an intercept to pair with.

sparse

Only FALSE is supported. The argument is there so that the function can be named in options(contrasts = ...) or set with contrasts(x) <- "contr_sum_zero".

Value

A matrix with one row per level and \(K - 1\) columns. Columns are orthonormal and every column sums to zero. With contrasts = FALSE, the \(K x K\) identity matrix.

Details

With sum-to-zero contrasts the model estimates the effect of each level relative to the average level, instead of relative to a reference level. R's stats::contr.sum() does this by setting the last level to minus the sum of the others. Normal priors on the coefficients then give the last level a larger prior variance than the others: \(K - 1\) times larger for \(K\) levels, three times larger with four items. With little data the prior is then not the same for all levels.

contr_sum_zero() returns orthonormal contrasts (a normalised Helmert basis). They describe the same sum-to-zero effects, but independent normal priors on the coefficients give every level the same prior variance. This is the coding used by Stan's sum_to_zero_vector type (Morris, 2025), which brms does not offer directly.

A normal(0, s) prior on the coefficients gives each level effect a prior SD of \(s \sqrt{(K - 1) / K}\). For a prior SD of \(\sigma\) per level, use \(s = \sigma \sqrt{K / (K - 1)}\). For example, with four levels and \(\sigma = 1\), use normal(0, 1.15).

The item and facet extractors in this package read the contrasts stored with the model data, so the level effects are reported on the original scale whatever contrasts were used.

References

Morris, M. (2025). The sum-to-zero constraint in Stan. Stan case study. https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/case-studies/sum_to_zero_vector.html

See also

stats::contr.sum(), stats::contrasts()

Examples

contr_sum_zero(4)
#>         [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
#> 1 -0.7071068 -0.4082483 -0.2886751
#> 2  0.7071068 -0.4082483 -0.2886751
#> 3  0.0000000  0.8164966 -0.2886751
#> 4  0.0000000  0.0000000  0.8660254

# The implied prior covariance of the level effects is proportional to
# diag(K) - 1/K: equal variances, equal negative correlations
H <- contr_sum_zero(c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
round(H %*% t(H), 3)
#>       A     B     C     D
#> A  0.75 -0.25 -0.25 -0.25
#> B -0.25  0.75 -0.25 -0.25
#> C -0.25 -0.25  0.75 -0.25
#> D -0.25 -0.25 -0.25  0.75

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
d <- data.frame(...)  # long data: id, item, rater, response
contrasts(d$item) <- contr_sum_zero(levels(d$item))
fit <- brms::brm(
  response ~ 1 + item + (1 | rater) + (1 | id),
  data = d, family = brms::acat(),
  prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1.15), class = b)
)
} # }
